To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

autoxidation of highly branched isoprpenoid (HBI)-triene lipids is faster than that of polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) lipids in marine sediments, and that the autoxidative products of HBI lipids may be used as tracers of autoxidative diagenesis.

the highly branched isomerization products of the highly branched alkenes are not autoxidation or photooxidation products of the highly unsaturated alkenes, but rather products of a radical chain reaction of a precursor that is not yet identified.

the autoxidative reactivity of highly branched isopenoid (HBI), a group of alkenes produced by diatoms and used as a proxy to reconstruct past sea surface temperatures (SST), is strongly dependent on the number of tri-unsaturated carbon-carbon bonds and the position of bis-allylic positions in the molecules, while mono- and diunsaturated HBIs are much less reactive and thus better preserved in marine sediments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new analytical techniques for the study of the reactivity of HBI towards auto- and photooxidation.
the reactivity of highly branched isopenoid (HBI), a class of alkenes produced by marine algae, towards photo- and autoxidative processes.
the reactivity of HBI alkanes towards autoxidization and photooxidation, which are important abiotic processes leading to the formation of HBI degradation products in the marine environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
autoxidation of highly branched isopenoid alkenes is not a major degradation process in sediments, but it is a significant process in marine surface waters.
HBI alkenols are highly reactive towards autoxideation and photooxidation.

the autoxidative reactivity of HBI alkanes increases with the number of double bonds and the presence of bis-allylic positions, while photooxidative reactivity depends on the presence of one or several double bonds conjugated with the carbonyl group.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the autoxidative reactivity of the different HBI alkenic moieties is in good agreement with their reactivity in photooxidation processes, but the reactivity of the bis-allylic positions is much more pronounced in autoxidation.

the autoxidative and photooxidative reactivity of the HBI alkenols is highly dependent on the number of tri-allylic positions, and to a lesser extent, on the number of double bonds, and on the presence of bis-allylic positions in the molecule.
autoxidation of HBI alkanes is a fast and effective process, which is favoured by the presence of bis-allylic and tri-substituted carbon-carbon double bonds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HBI alkenols are particularly reactive towards auto- and photooxidative degradation, and thus should be carefully considered when using HBI alkenones as biomarkers of sea surface temperature.

HBI trienes are highly reactive towards both autoxidation (in the dark) and photooxidation (under UV irradiation), and therefore should be considered as sensitive biomarkers of recent organic matter inputs.

the autoxidative reactivity of HBI alkanes can be used to identify the most reactive ones, which may be preferentially degraded in the water column and in marine sediments, and thus be less abundant in the sedimentary record.
